tasks.title: ANTARTICA GIVES UP ITS SECRETS
body: Scientists find new volcanoes beneath vast ice sheet Scientists have uncovered the largest volcanic region on Earth ‒ two kilometres below the surface of the vast ice sheet that covers west Antarctica.

The project, by Edinburgh University researchers, has revealed almost 100 volcanoes ‒ with the highest ones as tall as Mount Eiger, which towers almost 4,000 metres above Switzerland. The project leader, glacier expert Robert Bingham says this huge region is likely to have more volcanoes than east Africa's volcanic ridge, currently considered the densest concentration of volcanoes in the world.

The big questions are: How active are these volcanoes? And how many lie below the ice? This second question was originally asked by the team's youngest member, Van Wyk de Vries, an undergraduate at the university's school of geosciences and a self-confessed volcano fanatic. He set up the project with the help of Bingham. In the study they analysed measurements made by previous surveys which involved the use of radar, carried by planes or land vehicles, to survey strips of the west Antarctic ice.

The results were then compared with satellite and database records and geological information from other surveys. After the team had put together the results, it reported a staggering 91 previously unknown volcanoes, adding to the 47 others that had been discovered over the previous century of exploring the region. "We were amazed," Bingham said. "We had not expected to find anything like that number. We also suspect there are even more on the bed of the sea."

The discovery is particularly important because the activity of these volcanoes could have crucial implications for the rest of the planet. "If one of these volcanoes were to erupt, it could further destabilise some of West Antarctica's ice sheets, already affected by global warming. Meltwater flowing into the Antarctic ocean could provoke sea level rises intensifying those that are already affecting our oceans," said Bingham.

tasks.title: LET'S SAVE MAYA ANGELOU FROM FAKE QUOTES
body: "A bird doesn't sing because it has an answer, it sings because it has a song."

A thought-provoking sentiment, I'm sure you'd agree. You might even be tempted to quote it. That impulse certainly struck the US postal service, who in 2015 put it out on a stamp bearing the face of Maya Angelou, the world-famous writer, professor, former dancer, calypso singer, filmmaker and civil rights activist, who died the previous year.

The only problem? She didn't write it. Dr Maya Angelou was chosen as an official poet by the UN. Her seven memoirs have sold millions of copies around the world. She is a cultural icon – and among the world's most misquoted women. The US postal service defended the mistake by saying the quote was "associated" with Angelou, and that she used it in a 2013 interview. It could also have pointed the finger at the then President Barack Obama, who also attributed the line to Angelou while handing out the 2013 National Medal of Arts. The phrase was traced to a children's author named Joan Walsh Anglund, and her 1967 book, A Cup of Sun. Anglund was kind, saying: "I love Angelou's books, of course. I think it easily happens sometimes that people hear something, and it goes into their subconscious without them realising it." But not everyone feels able to shrug off such mistakes. For some, fighting misquotes becomes almost a life's work. Gregory Sullivan, who runs the Quote Investigator (QI) website, is one such figure. "Some of the massive quotation websites are filled with misinformation," he told the BBC. "These sites make the problem worse because many people incorrectly assume that large, professional-looking websites must contain valid data. The mission of QI is to provide information that is current, thorough, and very carefully documented." Sullivan writes with a pseudonym under which he wrote the book Hemingway Didn't Say That: The Truth Behind Familiar Quotations. So why do people keep pinning quotes on Maya Angelou? Basically, because the lines she did write were so good. Her quotability makes her a magnet for misquotation. Got a wise and compassionate line with no recorded owner? Just say it was Maya Angelou, the logic runs. Unless it's too spiritual, in which case try Gandhi or Mother Theresa. Or too sarcastic, when the obvious candidates are Oscar Wilde, Mark Twain or Winston Churchill. All eminently quotable men and women – and too dead to disclaim the words they never said.

Summary A 2015 stamp had Maya Angelou's picture on it and a sentence that the {{0}} thought was by her. She is very popular and many people read her books, yet she is often {{18}}. Strangely enough, this even happened at an award-giving ceremony in the US in {{19}}. The sentence "A bird doesn't sing because it has an answer, it sings because it has a song" actually first appeared in a(n) {{20}}, but the {{21}} didn't sound too upset about the whole thing.

Anyone wanting to trace a quote to its genuine source can consult {{22}}, a website that promises to give accurate data. The man behind it, {{23}}, is determined to correct misinformation spread by quotation websites. Apart from Maya Angelou, people like Mother Theresa or Winston Churchill, among others, are frequently misquoted, too; the {{24}} one often credited with quite biting remarks.

tasks.title: TYPEWRITER'S PROMISE OF A SIMPLER LIFE
body: Like-the clip-clop of horses' hooves on city streets or the crackle when a vinyl LP reaches the end, it is a sound that almost but never quite vanished. Now the clatter of typewriter keys has become the latest echo from the pre-digital world to be heard again.

The price of vintage manual typewriters has increased dramatically as authors, poets, lovers and even fed-up parents discover the delights of "slow writing". For most it is less about nostalgia and more about the need to escape the "noise" of email, social media and the internet.
The typewriter revolution began in the United States but has spread to Britain, where dozens of old machines are being restored every week.

Repairmen are being persuaded to come out of retirement to help to feed demand from a generation that never heard the ping of a typewriter bell. Tom Knowles, 59, did his apprenticeship in typewriter repair over 40 years ago. He has never been so busy supplying spare parts and repairing vintage Olivettis.

"People imagine my customers must be over 70 and can't get on with computers, but the reality is that most of them are under 30. A generation has suddenly discovered manual typewriters and thinks they are very cool," he said.

The typewriter's best known enthusiast is the actor Tom Hanks, who has a collection of more than a hundred. He has just finished a collection of short stories called Uncommon Type, each one featuring a different typewriter.

Mr Knowles said that people had gone back to manual typewriters because they found computers and smartphones, with their multiple functions, too distracting. "A manual typewriter is a single purpose machine, it does nothing else. Because it doesn't have a delete or a correction key it concentrates your mind more on what you're writing."
Philip Chapman, from Wiltshire, sells about 500 machines a year through his website at up to £350 each. Mr Chapman said: "We sell a lot to creative writers."

They also sell to parents who want to get their child away from their smartphone or tablet. "There are boys, particularly, who are not interested in creative writing until you put a mechanical typewriter in front of them," Mr Chapman said. "Suddenly they go 'wow' and the next moment they are writing."
